prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Where, Mazda, Peshawar

outputs.L1: Where am I going today—if I am going anywhere at all—without my soul, that bird whose name is unreadable, unheard, having wandered off once more, convinced it is more than a mere word? Do we travel far from each other today, I wonder—I in my pre-owned Mazda, radio humming with news like a disturbed wasps' nest, my Peshawar, my Rupert Murdoch, all my guilty Murdochs? My destination resembles a homestead built of fallen maple leaves—three leaves arranged into a tipi by a five-year-old's careful hands, a dwelling place where, should I wish, I might set down my human rights while my soul journeys far from its moorings, lost awhile on its own private, unaccompanied pilgrimage. The notion of living forever is, for my wanderer, no eternity at all, but merely a wish—the bird's desire to fly, embroidered in solitude within the borders of a tapestry, far from some witch-queen's cackle, far from that sorceress disguised as a sparrowhawk, woven from dark thread by a Flemish peasant's hands. How far is too far, you ask? A little folly carries one a long way, I'd say; but a great deal collapses in its tracks.
outputs.L2: Where might I be headed today—assuming I'm headed anywhere—now that my soul has slipped away once more, that elusive bird whose name defies both sight and sound, convinced it amounts to something beyond mere language? Are we drifting apart today, my soul and I? I sit here in my secondhand Mazda, the radio buzzing with news like a disturbed hornet's nest, filled with Peshawar and Rupert Murdoch, all my complicit Murdochs. My intended destination resembles a small dwelling constructed from fallen maple leaves—three leaves arranged into a tiny tipi by a child's careful hands, a shelter where I might set down my human rights while my soul roams distant from home, momentarily adrift on its own exclusive journey. Immortality, for this wandering spirit, isn't really about forever—it's simply the bird's longing to fly, embroidered in isolation somewhere within a tapestry's edges, far removed from a wicked queen's laughter, far from that same witch disguised as a hawk, stitched from somber thread by the hands of a Flemish farmworker. You might ask how far is too far? I'd answer that a touch of foolishness carries one surprisingly far, while excess collapses instantly.
outputs.L3:
# On the Wandering Soul

Can I go anywhere today without my soul? That errant bird has wandered off again, flown from its perch on my shoulder, convinced somehow that it is more than mere language, more than the word we use to name whatever flickers behind the eyes. It believes itself real in a way that unsettles me, this small feathered thing that will not stay put.

So my body goes on without it. I drive my pre-owned Mazda through the ordinary traffic of the day, the radio murmuring its litany of the world's business—Peshawar again, and Rupert Murdoch's empire creaking somewhere in the news—while I nod along, half-listening, entirely present in the driver's seat. But the soul, meanwhile, has embarked on its own itinerary, a journey "highly privatized," unlisted, unbookable, answerable to no schedule but its own.

I imagine, for it, a resting place: a small shelter built from fallen maple leaves, heaped and leaned together the way a child might construct a tipi in the backyard, all amber and rust-colored, fragile and temporary. This is where my "human rights" might pause and wait—patient, folded up small—while the soul goes roaming, unaccountable, elsewhere.

And where does it go? I picture its flight as a kind of escape, as though fleeing a witch queen who has taken the shape of a sparhawk, some menacing figure stitched into the corner of an old Flemish tapestry, all thread and shadow and old malice. But this flight is not born of any grand hope, not a bid for immortality or a desperate clutch at eternal life. It is smaller than that—a fleeting wish, a whim, gone as soon as it arrives.

And perhaps this is the lesson in it: that a little foolishness, taken in modest doses, is what carries us through—sustains us, even, across the long unremarkable stretches of our days. But indulge too much, chase the wish too far, and the fall comes quickly, without warning, the way all excess eventually collapses under its own weight.
outputs.L4:
# Unnamed Flight

I.

Somewhere between the merge lane and the radio's drone,
I have already left my body—
a small grey bird lifting off the dashboard,
unnamed, unclaimed, circling above the traffic
like a thought too shy to land.

The news reads itself in someone else's voice.
I nod. I signal. I am here
and also nowhere,
watching my hands hold the wheel
the way you'd watch a stranger's hands
perform a task you used to know.

II.

Later: the guilty hour. Chips, a rerun,
the phone's blue glow inside a dark room.
The bird returns, perches on the lamp,
watches me watch myself
being watched by no one.
This is freedom, I think—
or its cheap cousin,
the kind you buy in fifteen-minute increments
between obligations.

III.

I dream of a tapestry, medieval, moth-eaten at the border—
a hunter, a stag, a woman half-turned to leave the frame.
I recognize her.
She has my mother's hands, my sister's silence,
a green thread where her mouth should be.
Is she a witch, disguised as patience?
Is she the soul, disguised as woman,
disguised as thread,
disguised as something that will fray
if you look too long?

I wake still tangled in the weave.

IV.

The bird does not come back right away.
I drive to work. I answer emails.
Somewhere it is circling something—
a graveyard, maybe, or a childhood house,
or nothing, just the middle distance
where lost things go to practice being lost.

I begin to understand:
if it never returns, I am only weather,
only the shape a life makes
when nobody is steering it.
But if it never leaves,
I am only meat and calendar,
a body clocking in.

V.

So let the bird go, some nights.
Let it forget my name in the dark above the streetlights,
let it taste whatever thin freedom
exists north of the self.

But call it home before the frost.
Before the tapestry unravels past repair,
before the witch stops pretending
and starts to simply be the wound.

A little foolishness keeps the blood warm.
Too much, and you wake up
already a story
someone else is telling
about a woman who used to live here,
who used to fly,
who forgot, one autumn,
to come back down.
outputs.L5:
# Mazda Comes to Peshawar

For decades, residents of Peshawar seeking a new Mazda vehicle faced a common question: where exactly could they find an authorized dealership offering these Japanese-engineered cars? The historic city, nestled near the Khyber Pass, has long been a commercial hub for the region, yet international automotive brands often established their presence more slowly here compared to cities like Karachi, Lahore, or Islamabad.

Mazda's growing popularity in Pakistan reflects the brand's reputation for reliable engineering, fuel efficiency, and distinctive design philosophy known as "Kodo." As demand increased across the country, dealerships began appearing in secondary cities, and Peshawar eventually saw the establishment of showrooms catering to customers interested in models ranging from the compact Mazda 2 to the more robust CX-5 and BT-50 pickup trucks.

For potential buyers in Peshawar, locating a dealership typically means searching in commercial areas along major roads such as University Road, Jamrud Road, or the Ring Road, where many automotive showrooms cluster. These locations offer not just sales but also servicing, genuine spare parts, and warranty support—crucial factors for buyers considering a significant purchase.

The question of "where" also extends beyond physical dealerships. Prospective customers often research online first, checking official distributor websites, social media pages, and local classified platforms to compare prices, financing options, and available inventory before visiting in person.

For a city with Peshawar's rich trading history and its population's practical needs—navigating sometimes challenging terrain, valuing durability, and seeking value for money—Mazda's offerings have found a niche market. Whether it's a small business owner needing a dependable pickup truck or a family seeking a comfortable sedan, the availability of authorized Mazda dealerships in Peshawar represents the broader trend of global automotive brands expanding their footprint into Pakistan's secondary urban centers, meeting local demand where it exists rather than requiring customers to travel to larger metropolitan areas.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal stream-of-consciousness poem about a soul that wanders away from its owner during a mundane car commute.
counterfactuals.output:
# Departure

Somewhere between the third red light and the radio's
static hum, I slipped out through the crack in the window,
not much wider than a held breath, and nobody noticed—
least of all him, my driver, my tenant, my borrowed coat
of bone and blinking, still gripping the wheel like a man
who believes in destinations.

I float above the overpass. The cars beneath are beetles
carrying their pilots to appointments with forgetting.
I see him back there, still, in seat 4B of his own life,
humming along to a jingle he'll despise by evening,
unaware that the thing which makes his humming *mean*
has drifted up like smoke from a cigarette he doesn't smoke.

Time moves differently up here—
not moves, exactly, more like it *pools*,
the way rain pools in the dented hood of a car
that's been through something and kept driving anyway.

I remember (do souls remember? I'm making this up
as I float) I remember being pinned to his ribs like a moth
to corkboard, quivering each time he almost said the true thing
to the woman at the coffee shop, the one with the gap-toothed
smile that made his chest do its small collapse—

I was there for that. I flinched for both of us.

But now: no ribs. No collapsing chest. Just the long gray
ribbon of the interstate unspooling like a thought
that never finishes itself, and streetlights blinking on
like the world's slowest applause, and somewhere in there
he's checking his mirrors, merging, existing
in the particular loneliness of forward motion
without knowing he's now just motion, forward,
nothing steering the steering.

I could go back. I think I could.
There's a thread, gossamer, a tether
made of the specific blue of his childhood bicycle
and the smell of his mother's kitchen on Sundays
and every time he almost cried at movies but didn't—

but the sky keeps opening like a door held by wind,
and the clouds are doing that thing where they look
like every animal you've ever loved,
and honestly—

honestly it's nice out here.
No appointments.
No merging.
Just the long
unbodied
hum
of everything
that ever wanted
to be elsewhere,

floating,

while somewhere below,
a man arrives home,
parks the car,
and sits for one strange moment
before going inside—
not knowing why,
exactly,
he suddenly feels
so
light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem blending news headlines, personal identity, and medieval tapestry imagery, with long run-on sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thread Count**

I am woven into the same loom that reports six dead in a factory collapse and the unicorn kneeling in his pen of pomegranate trees, both of us stitched by hands that will never be named, and I scroll past *BREAKING* the way medieval eyes must have scanned the millefleur background for the one flower that meant something, the *rue* for regret, the *columbine* for folly, the *strawberry* for a righteousness nobody living could afford, and somewhere between the alert on my phone and the alert stitched into wool—*the hunters have found the beast, the hounds are loosed, the horns cry out*—I am trying to locate myself, am I the maiden who tames him with her lap, am I the spear, am I the small dog barking uselessly at the edge of the hunt, because the headline says *inflation cools* the way the tapestry says *the unicorn is not dead, only captive, only chained loosely enough to seem willing,* and isn't that also me, loosely chained to a name my mother gave me, to a gender assigned before I could refuse it, to a citizenship that is also a kind of gold thread pulling taut across a field of blue, and the news says *storm approaching landfall* and the tapestry says *and lo the beast lay down among the flowers as if this had always been his kingdom,* and I want to ask which century I am actually living in because grief has the same weight whether it comes stitched in silk or pushed through a notification, whether the body falls in Aleppo or in Bruges, whether the woman weeping is woven in wool dyed with madder root or is my own face reflected dim in a screen at 2 a.m., because identity, I am learning, is not a single thread but the whole warp, the vertical structure you can't see once the weaving's done, the part that holds everything else in tension so the picture can exist at all, so that when they say *who are you* I want to answer *I am the space between the deer and the arrow, I am the golden collar that says both captured and beloved, I am the headline and the herald, I am not yet finished being made*—and the loom keeps clacking somewhere underneath the century, underneath the feed, underneath the four hundred dead in a headline I already forgot the name of, and still the flowers keep blooming in the background, threaded in by some anonymous hand who never once believed she was making anything sacred, only surviving the winter, only feeding her children, only trying, the way I am trying, to be one bright particular color in a field too vast for any single eye to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract poem exploring the tension between the self and the soul, incorporating references to Rupert Murdoch and a Flemish tapestry.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thread and Signal**

I am woven from someone else's loom,
the self a chyron scrolling beneath the soul's
slow unicorn, captured in a garden
of millefleurs that never bloomed for me.

Somewhere a tower broadcasts
what I should call belonging—
Murdoch's static hums beneath my sternum,
a second heartbeat made of ratings,
telling me which grief to feel by Tuesday.

The soul does not watch television.
It sits instead inside the tapestry's blue field,
stitched too tight to reach the remote,
listening to gold thread fray
into something that might be prayer
or might be static
or might be the same frequency
wearing two disguises.

*Who owns the image of the wound?*

The self signs contracts with its face.
The soul just bleeds in wool and silk,
horizontal, patient, Flemish,
undated by the weavers who forgot
their names inside the border's ivy—
so much like forgetting
which part of me is renting space
inside the other.

News at eleven: a boy became a market.
News at eleven: a soul became a hashtag
trending underneath the hunted beast
that kneels, forever, in the maiden's lap,
threaded shut, its wound a single knot
of red that someone tied
five hundred years ago
and called it finished.

I am not finished.
I am the channel changing
mid-thought, mid-thread,
the self reaching for the clicker
while the soul keeps weaving backward,
undoing empires
one gold stitch
at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental poetry using birds as a metaphor for the soul, mixing modern anxieties (media, driving) with folklore imagery like witches and sparhawks.
counterfactuals.output:
**MURMURATION (for the thing that leaves the body at 3 a.m.)**

i.

They said the soul was a wren once,
small enough to slip through a keyhole,
small enough to die of cold in a fist.

Now it's something else—
gray, spliced, blinking
between four bars of signal and none,

a starling made of pixels,
flocking toward the blue light
that never sets, never says *sleep now, small one,*

only *refresh. refresh. refresh.*

ii.

*recalculating*

the GPS voice is a new kind of hex,
flat and county-fair friendly,
guiding the body down roads
the soul does not recognize as home—

turn left where the hawthorn used to be,
turn left where the old woman burned,
merge onto the highway that ate the orchard,

*in two hundred feet, you have arrived.*

but arrived where. but arrived as what.

iii.

Grandmother called it a sparhawk,
the thing that comes for the soul-bird
mid-flight, no warning, talons
already in the feathers before the shadow lands—

she said *don't watch the news at night,
it circles like that, it waits above the field
of your sleeping and takes what's smallest first.*

I did not listen. I have a phone
that glows like a familiar,
that perches on the nightstand
and watches me back.

iv.

*breaking:*
*breaking:*
*breaking:*

the wren is breaking.
the starling is breaking.
somewhere a woman is being called
a witch again, online, in comments,
for keeping birds, for keeping quiet,
for driving too slow on a road
that used to be a footpath
that used to be a woods
that used to be
enough.

v.

I drive at night to feel my body
still belongs to me and not the feed—

headlights catching something small
crossing the yellow line, low,
fast, a shape too quick to name—

sparrow. soul. sparhawk.
static. the same old spell
in a new tongue:

*something is hunting you
and you have named it convenience.*

vi.

Let the folklore back in
through the cracked window,
let it smell like rain and iron,
let the crows return to the wires
instead of the algorithm,

let the soul be a bird again—
not a notification,
not a blue light in a dark room,
not a location pin dropped
on a map of your own leaving—

let it be feathers.
let it be flight.
let it, for once,
outrun the hawk.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, imagistic prose poem in first person that questions how far one can separate from their own soul, using unusual juxtapositions of pop culture and myth.
counterfactuals.output:
# Distance from the Marrow

I have tried to leave myself in a gas station off I-40, tried to slip out the back like a debt unpaid, but the soul is a dog that finds its way home from three states over, paws bloodied by asphalt and neon signage, by every Waffle House sign blinking its yellow scripture into the dark.

How far can a thing travel from its own hum? Orpheus turned around because he could not bear the silence of not-looking, and I understand this — I check my phone in the middle of prayer, I want to see if the underworld texted back. My soul is Eurydice and also the snake and also the terrible urge to glance behind me at a life I'm still dragging like a wedding train through mud.

They say Achilles was dipped in the river except for his heel — I think we are all dipped except for the one place where the actual self leaks out, unprotected, and mine is shaped like a Blockbuster card in a drawer I can't throw away, magnetic strip worn smooth as a saint's touched foot. I keep it as a relic. I keep it as proof that once I belonged to a version of forever that had a return date.

You can put three thousand miles between yourself and your mother's voice and still hear her saying your whole name like a verdict. You can change your name the way Persephone changes address twice a year, wife of winter, daughter of green, and still the pomegranate seeds sit in your stomach like small red moons pulling every tide you didn't consent to.

I have watched my hands do things — sign forms, hold strangers, dial numbers — while some other part of me sat in the passenger seat of a Trans Am parked permanently in 1987, radio on, waiting for a song that already ended. This is the self that doesn't commute. This is the self that Icarus never really lost when he fell — the wax melted but the wanting stayed exactly the same altitude, hovering above the sea like a UPC code God forgot to scan.

Can you outrun your soul? Ask the sneakers Forrest Gump wore down to nothing, still moving, still some part of him standing still at that bench, holding a box of chocolates like a communion he wasn't sure he was allowed to take.

I think the soul is the return address you can't erase no matter how many times you send yourself somewhere else. I think it waits at the door like a golden retriever and also like the Minotaur — patient, hungry, only violent if you keep denying the shape of the maze is something you built yourself, brick by brick, mixtape by mixtape, prayer by unanswered prayer.

I have gone as far as Tulsa. I have gone as far as forgetting my own middle name in a job interview. Still, some nerve ending in me lights up every time a particular chord progression plays, some 90s-VHS-tracking-line version of my soul rolling over in its sleep, saying: *there you are. I never left. You're the one who kept almost leaving.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
